summary: This proposed standard defines a set of new properties for iCalendar data and extends the use of some existing properties to the entire iCalendar object. These additions let calendar items carry richer information.

eli5.summary: Calendar events are small text records. This adds some new fields, like extra labels, so a calendar can store more details about events.

subtitle: New calendar-wide properties and parameters for iCalendar: names, colors, images, conference links and more.

tldr.problem: Vendors had been adding ad hoc extensions to iCalendar, and some features, such as naming a whole calendar or attaching conference details, had no standard form.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC standardizes a set of properties (NAME, REFRESH-INTERVAL, SOURCE, COLOR, IMAGE, CONFERENCE) and parameters (DISPLAY, EMAIL, FEATURE, LABEL). It also lets several existing properties appear on the whole calendar object.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 5545, registers everything with IANA, and changes the advice on building UID values so they do not leak private information.

today: RFC 7986 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It updates RFC 5545.

sections.title: Why New Properties
sections.content:
iCalendar (RFC 5545) represents calendar data, and with iTIP (RFC 5546) it handles scheduling between calendar users. Vendors had added extension elements, as that specification allows.

RFC 7986 collects a number of these ad hoc extensions and uses the IANA registry capability from RFC 5545 to register standard versions with clear definitions. It also adds some new elements for features that vendors had recently requested.
sections.eli5: Many people invented their own extra boxes on the calendar form. This RFC picks the useful ones and makes them official so everyone fills them in the same way.

sections.title: Safe Extension Properties
sections.content:
Every iCalendar property has a default value type, used when no VALUE parameter is present. A generator that does not know a new property's default might treat a URI value as TEXT and backslash-escape a comma in it, which would make the URI invalid.

To avoid this, the RFC recommends that all properties not defined in RFC 5545 always include a VALUE parameter if the type is other than TEXT. The new properties use the phrase "no default" to say that VALUE has to be included.
sections.eli5: If a new box does not say what kind of thing goes in it, a program might scramble it. So the new boxes always say what they hold.

sections.title: Calendar-Level and New Properties
sections.content:
Several existing properties may now appear on the whole calendar object: DESCRIPTION, UID, LAST-MODIFIED, URL and CATEGORIES. UID then identifies the calendar, for example to spot duplicate calendar streams, and LAST-MODIFIED helps find its most recent version. When CATEGORIES appears several times, the categories are the union of all the values.

New properties:

  • NAME: the name of the calendar. It can repeat, but each copy must be in a different language.
  • REFRESH-INTERVAL: a suggested minimum polling interval, given as a positive DURATION. Clients SHOULD use it to limit polling.
  • SOURCE: a URI where updated calendar data can be fetched. It differs from URL, which gives an alternative representation rather than the original location.
  • COLOR: a CSS3 color name that clients MAY use as the background color of events or tasks.
  • IMAGE: an image given as a URI or inline base64 binary data, for the calendar or for events, to-dos and journal entries.
  • CONFERENCE: a URI for accessing a conferencing system, which can be repeated on an event or to-do.
sections.eli5: A calendar can now have its own name, a color, a picture, a link to fetch fresh updates, and a way to join an online meeting.

sections.title: New Property Parameters
sections.content:
Four parameters are added.

  • DISPLAY says how an IMAGE is shown: BADGE (the default), GRAPHIC, FULLSIZE or THUMBNAIL. Clients and servers MUST NOT display any image for a value they do not recognize.
  • EMAIL gives an email address for an ORGANIZER or ATTENDEE whose calendar user address is not easy to match against an address book. Clients SHOULD NOT include it when it matches the calendar user address.
  • FEATURE describes what a conference offers: AUDIO, CHAT, FEED, MODERATOR, PHONE, SCREEN or VIDEO. MODERATOR marks a URI that is specific to the conference owner, such as a moderator access code.
  • LABEL is a human-readable label that tells similar properties apart. The RFC expects other extensions to reuse it.
sections.eli5: These are little notes attached to a box: how to show the picture, what the meeting link can do, and a friendly name so you can tell two links apart.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
Several properties point to external URIs, which could hold malicious content or be used to track access. Clients SHOULD get the user's permission before dereferencing them, and calendar publishers MUST use HTTPS to protect subscriber privacy.

A very short REFRESH-INTERVAL, such as one second, could be used to cause rapid requests and a denial of service. Clients MUST throttle requests, and if the interval is shorter than once per day they SHOULD warn the user and allow a longer value. To prevent publishers tracking individuals through distinct values, clients SHOULD add or subtract a random amount of time when refreshing.

Moderator access codes in CONFERENCE properties must not be sent to attendees. Imported COLOR and IMAGE properties can produce a confusing display, so clients should let users remove or adjust them.
sections.eli5: A link in a calendar could lead somewhere bad or watch who clicks it. So the calendar should ask first, and should not ask a server for updates too often.

sections.title: Safer UID Values
sections.content:
The UID advice in RFC 5545 suggested using host names, IP addresses and domain names. The RFC says this is no longer good practice because it can leak information about a user, host or network.

It updates RFC 5545 so that UID values MUST NOT include any data that might identify a user, host, domain or other sensitive information. Calendar user agents are now RECOMMENDED to generate hex-encoded random UUIDs as defined in RFC 4122. Other opaque identifiers MUST be shorter than 255 octets and conform to the iana-token syntax.
sections.eli5: A calendar item's ID number should be random, not made from your computer's name, which could reveal things about you.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the new properties in the iCalendar "Properties" registry and the new parameters in the "Parameters" registry. It also added references to this document for the existing properties it updates.

Two new registries were created: "Display Types", initialized with BADGE, GRAPHIC, FULLSIZE and THUMBNAIL, and "Feature Types", initialized with the seven FEATURE values. Further values may be added using the process in RFC 5545.
sections.eli5: Official lists were set up so everyone can see which boxes and options exist, and new ones can be added by following the rules.

data.title: New iCalendar properties
data.code:
NAME:Company Vacation Days
REFRESH-INTERVAL;VALUE=DURATION:P1W
SOURCE;VALUE=URI:https://example.com/holidays.ics
COLOR:turquoise
CONFERENCE;VALUE=URI;FEATURE=CHAT;
 LABEL=Chat room:xmpp:chat-123@conference.example.com

items.title: DISPLAY
items.text: How an image is shown; BADGE by default.

items.title: EMAIL
items.text: An email address for an organizer or attendee.

items.title: FEATURE
items.text: What a conference offers, such as AUDIO or VIDEO.

items.title: LABEL
items.text: A human-readable label for a property.
